title: Worsening breathlessness in a 74-year-old retired meteorologist
desc: This station is a focused breathlessness history and cardiorespiratory examination of Adam Jung, a 74-year-old retired meteorologist seeing his GP. His breathlessness has worsened over years and is now brought on by walking 10 m. He has orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, exertional chest tightness and exertional dizziness with a brief blackout. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his ECG, chest X-ray report, blood results and echocardiogram report. They should classify him as NYHA class IV and diagnose heart failure with preserved ejection fraction caused by severe calcific aortic stenosis. They then arrange hospital care and heart team assessment for aortic valve replacement, explain the problem to Adam and safety-net.
focus: Dyspnoea: measuring breathlessness by what the patient can do, screening across systems with cluster questions and asking for the aortic stenosis triad, then recognising severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with HFpEF on the echo and planning valve replacement
diagnosis: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a general practice on the outskirts of Melbourne. Adam Jung is a 74-year-old retired meteorologist who has come in because his breathing is getting worse. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first and is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Jung and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his ECG, his chest X-ray report, his blood results and his echocardiogram report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Adam Jung, a 74-year-old retired meteorologist. Your date of birth is 9 June 1952. You are sitting up in the chair. Walking in from the waiting room made you a little short of breath, but you can talk in full sentences. You are matter-of-fact and a little frustrated. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "My breathing's getting worse, doctor. I just can't get a full breath in."

The breathlessness (give only when asked):

  • Onset and course: it started gradually a few years ago, when you were walking up the hill to the shops. Over the past two months it has been there all the time.
  • Quality: "I just can't get a full breath in."
  • How much you can do: for the last two years you have been very short of breath walking up the hill to the shops. In the past week you get breathless after about 10 m, walking to the letterbox.
  • What you have tried: "I've tried using my puffer but it doesn't work."
  • Worse: lying down. Better: nothing much, apart from stopping to rest.
  • Only if asked specifically (do not volunteer either):
    • Orthopnoea: for the past couple of weeks you have been sleeping propped up on three pillows because lying flat makes you breathless.
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea: several times recently you have woken in the night gasping and had to sit on the edge of the bed until it passed.
  • Impact: "It's just so hard to get around!"
  • What you think it is: "I'm not sure."

Other heart symptoms (only if asked about chest pain or fainting on exertion):

  • Chest pain on exertion: over the past few months, walking uphill brings on a tightness in the middle of your chest. It does not spread anywhere and goes after a few minutes' rest. You have never had it at rest.
  • Fainting on exertion: twice in the past couple of months, walking up the hill, you came over dizzy and had to sit down on a neighbour's front wall. The second time you think you blacked out for a second or two. You came round straight away with no injury and no confusion, and you did not tell anyone.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all are absent):

  • Heart failure: no ankle swelling that you have noticed, no cough, and no discomfort under your right ribs.
  • Heart attack or rhythm: no chest pain at rest, no sweating, no nausea. No palpitations or racing heart.
  • Infection or TB: no fever, chills or night sweats, no phlegm, no sharp pain on breathing in. No overseas travel and no contact with TB.
  • Airways and lung scarring: no wheeze, no long-term cough, no cough at night. Your work was in offices and at weather stations, with no dust, asbestos or chemical exposure.
  • Clot: no coughing up blood, no calf pain or swelling, no recent long trips, operations or time in bed.
  • Thyroid and blood: no tremor, no heat intolerance, no weight loss and no diarrhoea. No bleeding and no black stools. You are not especially tired, "just puffed".

Past medical history:

  • High blood pressure for 24 years. "The doctors are always telling me it's too high."
  • High cholesterol for 12 years, "so-so" control.
  • Asthma since childhood. You rarely need your puffer these days.
  • Hay fever.

Medications: amlodipine, atorvastatin, and a Ventolin puffer when needed. You don't know the doses. No other medicines or supplements. Allergies: none. Vaccinations: up to date.

Family history:

  • Your mother died of a heart attack at 72.
  • Your father had asthma from childhood.
  • Your sister has had angina since she was 58.
  • Your brother has had high blood pressure since he was 38.
  • Your children are healthy.

Social history:

  • Smoking: about half a pack a day from age 20. You stopped 10 years ago.
  • Alcohol: you never drink.
  • Exercise: you used to swim every week, but you can't manage it now.
  • Diet: home-cooked, but oily and salty, with plenty of white bread, rice and pasta.
  • Home: you live on the outskirts of Melbourne with your wife and your adult son, who has a disability and depends on you both. You help your wife lift and care for him. You have little outside support.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are not sure what is causing this. You are worried because you can't get around, and your wife can't care for your son on her own. You would like to know what is going on and to be able to breathe properly again.

Question to raise (near the end of Part 1, if not already covered): "Is it my asthma playing up? The puffer just isn't doing anything."

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: overweight older man sitting upright. Mildly breathless after the walk in, improving but not fully settling at rest, speaking in full sentences. Not cyanosed, not pale. Alert and oriented.
  • Vital signs (09:40): HR 86 beats/min, regular; BP 146/92 mmHg; RR 20/min; SpO2 95% on room air; temperature 36.6 °C. Weight 82 kg today; the practice record shows 79 kg three months ago. Height 175 cm.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds. No clubbing, no tar staining, no tremor.
  • Pulse: radial pulse regular. The radial and carotid pulses are small in volume and slow-rising.
  • Face and eyes: no conjunctival pallor, no central cyanosis, no lid lag.
  • Neck: JVP raised 4 cm above the sternal angle. The murmur is heard over both carotids. Trachea midline. No goitre.
  • Praecordium: apex beat in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line (not displaced). It is forceful and sustained (heaving). No thrill. A harsh grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur, late-peaking, loudest in the 2nd intercostal space at the right sternal edge and louder with him sitting forward in expiration. It radiates to both carotids and is also heard, more musical, at the apex. S2 is soft (A2 barely audible). An S4 is present. No diastolic murmur.
  • Chest: no hyperinflation. Fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. The right base is stony dull to percussion, with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. No wheeze, no bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft, liver edge not palpable, no right upper quadrant tenderness.
  • Legs and sacrum: no pitting oedema of the ankles, shins or sacrum. Calves soft, non-tender and equal in size.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms the patient's name and date of birth, explains confidentiality and gains consent for the history and examination.
Opens with an open question and builds rapport. Acknowledges how hard it is for him to get around, uses plain language and summarises back to him.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:

kids.x: Onset and course: came on gradually a few years ago walking to the shops, and has been constant for the past two months.
Quality ("can't get a full breath in"), and finds that his salbutamol puffer does not help.
Measures it by exercise tolerance, not a score out of 10: badly breathless up the hill to the shops over the past two years, and now after 10 m (to the letterbox) in the past week.
kids.d: A rating out of 10 on its own does not earn this item.

kids.x: Finds what makes it worse (lying down), its impact ("so hard to get around") and what he thinks it is (not sure).

check.x: Asks specifically about orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and finds both (three pillows; waking at night gasping).
check.d: Neither is volunteered. Credit only a specific question. "Is it worse at night?" alone does not release them.

check.x: Asks about exertional chest pain and exertional dizziness or syncope (the aortic stenosis triad). Finds central chest tightness walking uphill that settles with rest, and two episodes of dizziness on the hill, one with a brief blackout.
check.d: Both are given only if asked about chest pain and fainting or dizziness. Both questions are needed.

check.x: Uses cluster questions to screen differentials across systems:
check.d: Source marking: full credit for clusters covering at least 5 diagnoses from different systems, part credit for 4, minimal credit for 3. Items 6 and 7 count towards the cardiac clusters. Tick each sub-item covered with at least two questions.

kids.x: Other heart failure features: ankle swelling, dry cough, right upper quadrant discomfort (none).
ACS or arrhythmia (AF): chest pain at rest, sweating, nausea, palpitations (none).
Pneumonia or TB: fever, sputum, pleuritic pain, night sweats, travel or TB contact (none).
COPD, asthma or interstitial lung disease: wheeze, chronic cough or sputum, occupational dust or asbestos (none).
Pulmonary embolism: haemoptysis, calf pain or swelling, immobility, travel or surgery (none).
Thyrotoxicosis or anaemia: tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss; fatigue, bleeding, black stools (none).

check.x: Past medical history: poorly controlled hypertension for 24 years, hypercholesterolaemia for 12 years, childhood-onset asthma rarely needing his puffer, and hay fever.
Medications (amlodipine, atorvastatin, salbutamol as needed), allergies (none) and vaccinations (up to date).
Family history of premature or significant cardiovascular disease: mother died of AMI at 72, sister with angina from 58.
check.d: The other relatives (brother with hypertension, father with asthma, healthy children) are not required.

check.x: Takes a social history:
check.d: Diet and exercise (oily, salty diet; weekly swimming, now limited) are not required for this item.

kids.x: Smoking quantified: half a pack a day from 20, stopped 10 years ago (about 22 pack-years). Never drinks alcohol.
Home and supports: lives with his wife and a dependent adult son with a disability, whom he helps care for, with limited social support.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, worried about getting around and about who will care for his son, and asking whether it is his asthma.
Examination

General inspection, vital signs including SpO2, and weight. Finds him upright and mildly breathless after walking, with RR 20, SpO2 95% on room air, BP 146/92 and HR 86 regular. Notes his weight is up 3 kg in 3 months.
Assesses the radial and carotid pulse for rate, rhythm, volume and character. Finds a regular, small-volume, slow-rising pulse.
Assesses the JVP (raised 4 cm) and examines the hands, eyes and neck for clubbing, pallor, cyanosis, tremor and goitre (all normal).

Examines the praecordium. Finds a forceful, sustained, undisplaced apex beat and a harsh ejection systolic murmur loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space, louder sitting forward in expiration and radiating to the carotids, with a soft S2 and an S4.
check.d: Critical element: auscultates the aortic area and the carotids and reports the ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. The S2, S4 and apex findings are supporting.

check.x: Examines the chest front and back. Finds fine bibasal crackles and a stony dull right base with reduced breath sounds (effusion), and no wheeze.
Looks for oedema at the ankles, shins and sacrum (none), hepatomegaly (none) and calf swelling or tenderness (none).
Interpretation
ECG: sinus rhythm at 86 with left ventricular hypertrophy and a lateral strain pattern. No AF, no ST elevation, no Q waves.
Chest X-ray: identifies
check.d: Accept in the ISBAR assessment or in the diagnosis answer. Aortic valve calcification and the absence of hyperinflation are credited within items 27 and 28, not here.

kids.x: Pulmonary venous congestion with interstitial oedema (upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines).
Small bilateral pleural effusions, right larger than left, matching the stony dull right base.

check.x: Bloods: BNP 640 supports heart failure. Hb and TSH are normal, which excludes anaemia and thyrotoxicosis. Creatinine 118 (eGFR 52) and urea 9.1 are mildly impaired from baseline, which matters for diuretics and contrast for a valve work-up.
Echocardiogram, interpreted by morphology, severity and consequences:
check.d: Source marking: valve morphology, severity by Doppler (velocity, gradient, valve area) and consequences.

kids.x: Morphology: trileaflet, heavily calcified valve with severely reduced cusp opening, so calcific (degenerative) aortic stenosis.
Severity: peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg and valve area 0.7 cm², all in the severe range.
kids.d: Needs the word severe and at least two of the three parameters.

kids.x: Consequences: any two of concentric LVH, preserved ejection fraction (60%), raised filling pressure (diastolic dysfunction) and estimated PASP 51 mmHg (pulmonary hypertension).

check.x: Classifies him as NYHA class IV: breathless walking 10 m, and at rest lying flat and at night.
check.d: The source answer is class IV. Credit only class IV.

check.x: States the most likely diagnosis: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction caused by severe, symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis, with small bilateral pleural effusions. Justifies it from the exertional triad, orthopnoea and PND, the slow-rising pulse and murmur, the congestion and aortic valve calcification on X-ray, the BNP and the echo.
check.d: Credit aortic valve calcification on the X-ray here.

check.x: Gives at least two differentials, each with a feature for or against: coronary artery disease (exertional chest tightness and risk factors; coronary angiography still needed), COPD (22 pack-years; no wheeze or sputum, no hyperinflation on X-ray), asthma (salbutamol has no effect), HFrEF or other valve disease (EF 60%, only mild MR), PE (gradual course over years, no calf signs or haemoptysis).
check.d: The source's top three are congestive heart failure secondary to aortic stenosis, aortic stenosis or other valve disease, and COPD. Credit 'no hyperinflation on the X-ray' here.

check.x: Management

Confirms that Adam needs hospital care today (accepted by the cardiology registrar; direct admission, transferred by ambulance) for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with NYHA IV heart failure and exertional syncope. While he waits, keeps him upright and repeats observations.
check.d: An outpatient referral letter alone, or a routine echo review in weeks, does not earn this item.

check.x: Manages the congestion cautiously: loop diuretic (furosemide) with monitoring of weight, BP and UEC, avoiding over-diuresis, plus salt restriction and daily weights.
check.d: Accept in the management answer or the ISBAR recommendation. Optional, not required for the mark: blood pressure control titrated cautiously with cardiology (for example low-dose ACE inhibitor), avoiding hypotension; avoids or uses nitrates (including GTN) only with great caution, as they can cause syncope in severe AS.

check.x: Refers to the heart team for aortic valve replacement with a tissue (bioprosthetic) valve, either transcatheter (TAVI, often favoured at his age) or surgical (SAVR), with the choice depending on surgical risk, anatomy (transfemoral access, coronaries, aorta), frailty and his preference.
Arranges support for his son and wife before admission (for example family, a social worker, respite or Carer Gateway) and involves his wife in the plan.

Explains to Adam in plain words, in small chunks and checking understanding: the main valve out of the heart has become narrowed and stiff, so the heart muscle has thickened and stiffened and fluid backs up into the lungs. It is not his asthma, and the valve can be replaced.
Safety netting

Gives red flags in plain words: fainting or blacking out, chest pain that comes on at rest or does not settle within a few minutes of resting, breathlessness at rest or getting worse, being unable to lie down at all, and coughing up frothy or pink phlegm.
check.d: Credit at least three specific red flags, including fainting.

check.x: Says what to do: tell staff straight away while he waits here, and call 000 if any of these happen at home after discharge.

Advises him to avoid strenuous exertion (no hill walking, no swimming) and not to drive until he has been assessed and the valve has been treated (exertional syncope; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

part2.lead: After your examination your supervising GP called the cardiology registrar, who accepted Adam for admission. While the bed was arranged, the practice nurse recorded an ECG and the attached imaging, pathology and cardiology rooms completed a chest X-ray, bloods and echocardiogram. It is now 16:00 and the bed is ready. His observations at 15:50 were HR 86 regular, BP 144/90, RR 20, SpO2 95% on room air and temperature 36.6 °C. Here are his ECG, his chest X-ray report, his blood results and his echocardiogram report.
part2.patient:
Adam is present for question 4. If the candidate has not covered them, he asks:

  • "So it's not my asthma, then?"
  • "Can they fix it? Will I need my chest opened up?"

He listens closely and is relieved to hear the valve can be replaced, but says, "I can't just leave my wife on her own with our son."

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 09:55 today. Adam Jung, 74.

  • Rate: 86 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, with a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal (0°).
  • PR interval: 184 ms.
  • QRS: 104 ms. Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (S in V1 plus R in V5 = 42 mm). No pathological Q waves.
  • QTc: 448 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in I, aVL, V5 and V6 (repolarisation abnormality with LVH). No ST elevation.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.

Conclusion: sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and a lateral repolarisation (strain) pattern. No atrial fibrillation, no heart block, no acute ST elevation.
handover.model:
Read: sinus rhythm at 86, normal axis, and normal PR, QRS and QTc. LVH by voltage with lateral ST depression and T-wave inversion (strain pattern). No AF, no Q waves, no ST elevation.

For Adam: LVH fits a pressure-loaded left ventricle from aortic stenosis and long-standing poorly controlled hypertension. There is no arrhythmia such as AF to explain the decline. The strain changes make ischaemia hard to judge, and he has exertional chest tightness, so coronary disease is not excluded.

What it changes: it supports a cardiac cause. He will need coronary assessment (angiography) as part of the valve work-up. With no old ECG for comparison, it is a baseline.

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA and lateral, erect. Taken at 13:20 today.

Patient: Adam Jung, 74-year-old man.

Clinical details: progressive breathlessness over years, now on walking 10 m, with orthopnoea and PND. Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Dull right base. Ex-smoker. Hypertension.

Comparison: none available.

Technique: not rotated, adequate inspiration, adequately exposed.

Findings:

  • Airway and mediastinum: trachea central. The ascending aorta is prominent along the right upper mediastinum. Hila mildly prominent and indistinct, in keeping with vascular congestion.
  • Heart: cardiothoracic ratio about 0.49, heart size within normal limits, with a rounded left ventricular contour. Dense calcification projects over the aortic valve on the lateral view.
  • Lungs: upper lobe venous diversion. Septal (Kerley B) lines at both bases. No perihilar alveolar oedema, no focal consolidation, no mass. Lungs not hyperinflated, and the hemidiaphragms are not flattened.
  • Pleura and diaphragm: small right pleural effusion with a meniscus. The left costophrenic angle is minimally blunted, in keeping with a trace effusion. No pneumothorax. No free gas under the diaphragm.
  • Bones and soft tissues: degenerative change in the thoracic spine. No fracture.
  • Lines and devices: none.

Conclusion: pulmonary venous congestion with interstitial oedema and small bilateral pleural effusions (right larger than left). Aortic valve calcification with a prominent ascending aorta, suggesting aortic valve disease; correlate with echocardiography. No consolidation or hyperinflation.
handover.model:
Read: PA and lateral erect film of the correct patient, with adequate technique. Trachea central, ascending aorta prominent, hila congested. Heart size normal (CTR 0.49) with a rounded LV contour, and aortic valve calcification on the lateral view. Upper lobe diversion and Kerley B lines. Small right effusion and a trace left effusion. No alveolar oedema, consolidation, mass or hyperinflation. No pneumothorax, no free gas, no lines.

For Adam: the film shows interstitial pulmonary oedema with effusions, which fits his orthopnoea, PND, crackles and stony dull right base. The calcified valve and prominent ascending aorta (post-stenotic dilatation) point to aortic stenosis. A normal-sized heart does not exclude HFpEF: a concentrically hypertrophied ventricle often looks normal on X-ray. No hyperinflation argues against COPD.

What it changes: he is congested and needs diuresis. The echo will define the valve disease.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 13:40 today at the collection centre next door; urgent results phoned through at 15:30. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: BNP 640 ng/L, markedly raised. Creatinine 118 (baseline 102) with eGFR 52, and urea 9.1. Sodium and potassium normal. Hb 138 with a normal MCV, and normal white cell count and platelets. LFTs, albumin and TSH normal.

For Adam: the BNP strongly supports heart failure; a normal BNP would have made it unlikely. The mild rise in creatinine and urea fits reduced renal perfusion in heart failure. A normal Hb excludes anaemia, and a normal TSH excludes thyrotoxicosis, as contributors to his breathlessness. Normal LFTs show no significant hepatic congestion.

What it changes: these are baselines for diuresis, which needs close monitoring of electrolytes and renal function. His renal function also matters for the contrast used in the coronary angiogram and CT for the valve work-up.

rows.n: Acute presentation: BNP below 100 ng/L makes heart failure unlikely (non-acute threshold below 35 ng/L)

handover.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram report
handover.result:
Examination: transthoracic echocardiogram, 14:40 today. Adam Jung, 74. Height 175 cm, weight 82 kg (BSA 1.97 m²). Sinus rhythm at 84 during the study. Image quality good.

Clinical details: progressive exertional breathlessness, now on walking 10 m, with orthopnoea and PND, exertional chest tightness and exertional syncope. Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Slow-rising pulse.

Findings:

  • Left ventricle: normal cavity size. Concentric hypertrophy (septum 14 mm, posterior wall 13 mm). No regional wall motion abnormality. LVEF 60% (biplane Simpson's).
  • Diastolic function: impaired relaxation with raised filling pressure (average E/e' 16), grade II diastolic dysfunction.
  • Left atrium: moderately dilated (LA volume index 44 mL/m²).
  • Aortic valve: trileaflet, heavily calcified, with severely reduced cusp excursion. Peak transaortic velocity 4.6 m/s. Mean gradient 52 mmHg. Aortic valve area (continuity equation) 0.7 cm² (indexed 0.36 cm²/m²). Mild aortic regurgitation.
  • Aorta: aortic root normal. Ascending aorta mildly dilated at 41 mm.
  • Mitral valve: mild annular calcification and mild mitral regurgitation. No mitral stenosis.
  • Right heart: right ventricle normal in size and function (TAPSE 19 mm). Mild tricuspid regurgitation. Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 51 mmHg. Inferior vena cava dilated (22 mm) with less than 50% collapse on sniffing.
  • Pericardium and pleura: no pericardial effusion. Small right pleural effusion noted.

Conclusion: severe calcific aortic stenosis of a trileaflet valve (peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg, AVA 0.7 cm²). Concentric LV hypertrophy with preserved systolic function (LVEF 60%) and grade II diastolic dysfunction with raised filling pressure. Moderately dilated left atrium. Moderate pulmonary hypertension with a raised right atrial pressure. Findings consistent with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction secondary to severe aortic stenosis.
handover.model:
Read by the three steps:

  • Morphology: a trileaflet, heavily calcified valve with severely reduced opening, so calcific degenerative aortic stenosis (not bicuspid, and not rheumatic, as the mitral valve is spared).
  • Severity: peak velocity 4.6 m/s (severe is 4.0 or more), mean gradient 52 mmHg (severe is 40 or more) and AVA 0.7 cm² (severe is below 1.0), all concordant for severe aortic stenosis.
  • Consequences: concentric LVH with an EF of 60%, diastolic dysfunction with raised filling pressure, a dilated LA, PASP 51 mmHg, a raised RA pressure and a small right effusion.

For Adam: this confirms HFpEF caused by severe aortic stenosis. With breathlessness, angina and exertional syncope, he has all three classic symptoms. Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis carries a poor prognosis without valve replacement. EF 60% excludes HFrEF, and only mild mitral regurgitation means no other significant valve lesion.

What it changes: the cause is mechanical, so the definitive treatment is aortic valve replacement (TAVI or SAVR) after heart team assessment. In the meantime, the congestion needs cautious diuresis. The ascending aorta at 41 mm is noted for the heart team.

ask: You are now calling the cardiology registrar who has accepted Adam for admission. Please give an ISBAR handover of Adam, including your interpretation of these results.
What is Adam's NYHA class, what is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Adam, starting now here in general practice, including the definitive treatment.
Adam asks you what is wrong with his heart and how it can be fixed. Explain this to him, and tell him the warning signs to watch for and what to do.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student with the supervising GP. Adam Jung, 74.
  • Situation: severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with heart failure (preserved EF), NYHA IV. Accepted for admission today.
  • Background: breathlessness over years, now at 10 m. Orthopnoea, PND, exertional chest tightness, exertional syncope (brief blackout). Poorly controlled hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, childhood asthma; ex-smoker, 22 pack-years. Carer for his disabled son.
  • Assessment: obs stable on air (HR 86, BP 144/90, SpO2 95%). Slow-rising pulse, ESM to carotids, JVP +4, bibasal crackles, R effusion. Echo: severe calcific AS (Vmax 4.6, MG 52, AVA 0.7), EF 60%, LVH, raised filling pressure, PASP 51. CXR: interstitial oedema, effusions R>L. ECG: sinus, LVH with strain. BNP 640, eGFR 52.
  • Recommendation: admit for cautious diuresis and expedited heart team assessment for valve replacement.

NYHA class IV: breathless walking 10 m, and at rest lying flat and at night.

Most likely: HFpEF secondary to severe symptomatic calcific aortic stenosis, with small bilateral effusions. For it: the triad (breathlessness, exertional angina, exertional syncope), orthopnoea and PND, slow-rising pulse, ESM to the carotids, soft S2, congestion and valve calcification on the X-ray, BNP 640, and an echo showing severe AS with EF 60%.

At least two differentials, each with one feature for or against:

  • Coronary artery disease: exertional tightness, risk factors, family history. Angiography still needed.
  • COPD: 22 pack-years. Against: no wheeze or sputum, no hyperinflation.
  • Asthma: against: salbutamol has no effect.
  • HFrEF or other valve disease: against: EF 60%, only mild MR.
  • PE: against: gradual course, no calf signs or haemoptysis.

1. Today: cardiology has accepted him. Severe symptomatic AS with NYHA IV failure and syncope needs hospital today (direct admission, transferred by ambulance). Keep him upright, repeat observations; oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92%.
  2. HFpEF: cautious loop diuretic, avoiding over-diuresis (the ventricle depends on filling pressure). Monitor weight, BP, UEC. Salt and fluid restriction, daily weights. Blood pressure control titrated cautiously with cardiology (for example low-dose ACE inhibitor), avoiding hypotension; avoid nitrates (including GTN) or use only with great caution, as they can cause syncope in severe AS.
  3. Treat the cause: heart team assessment for aortic valve replacement, TAVI or SAVR with a tissue valve. Work-up includes coronary angiography and CT.
  4. Social: arrange care for his son (family, social worker, respite, Carer Gateway); involve his wife.
  5. Follow-up: GP review within a week of discharge.

• Explanation: in small chunks, without jargon, checking understanding. The main valve out of his heart has become narrow and stiff with calcium. His heart has had to squeeze harder, so the muscle has thickened and stiffened, and fluid backs up into his lungs. That is why he is breathless lying flat. It is not his asthma, which is why the puffer doesn't help. The valve can be replaced, often through a tube from the groin; the heart team will advise.
  • Red flags: fainting or blacking out; chest pain at rest or not settling with rest; breathlessness at rest or getting worse; unable to lie down at all; frothy or pink phlegm.
  • What to do: tell staff now while waiting; call 000 at home.
  • Activity and driving: no strenuous exertion, and no driving, until he has been assessed and the valve has been treated.

ddx.dx: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction secondary to severe calcific aortic stenosis
ddx.for: Breathlessness over years now at 10 m, orthopnoea and PND, exertional chest tightness and syncope, a slow-rising pulse, an ejection systolic murmur to the carotids, congestion with effusions on the X-ray, BNP 640, and severe AS with EF 60% on the echo.
Exertional central chest tightness settling with rest, poorly controlled hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, 22 pack-years, a mother who died of AMI and a sister with angina.
ddx.against: Severe aortic stenosis alone can explain the angina, there is no rest pain and no regional wall motion abnormality; coronary angiography is still needed.

ddx.for: About 22 pack-years of smoking and progressive exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: No chronic cough, sputum or wheeze, no hyperinflation on the X-ray, and the orthopnoea and PND point to the heart.

ddx.for: Childhood-onset asthma and hay fever, and he has been using his salbutamol puffer.
ddx.against: The puffer has no effect, there is no wheeze, and the breathlessness is worse lying flat.

ddx.dx: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, or another valve lesion
ddx.for: Hypertension, coronary risk factors and signs of congestion.
ddx.against: LVEF 60% with no regional wall motion abnormality, and only mild mitral and aortic regurgitation on the echo.

ddx.for: Breathlessness with a pleural effusion in an older man.
ddx.against: Gradual course over years, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf signs or immobility, and the echo and X-ray explain the picture.

guide:
Part 1 is set at about 09:30 in the consulting room. Give orthopnoea and PND only when the candidate asks about them specifically. Give the exertional chest tightness and the dizziness with a blackout only when the candidate asks about chest pain and about fainting or dizziness. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Item 8 follows the source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least five diagnoses from different systems, part credit for four, minimal credit for three. The orthopnoea, PND and triad questions in items 6 and 7 count as cardiac clusters. For the family history (item 11), only the mother's AMI and the sister's angina are needed.

Part 2 is set at 16:00 the same day. After Part 1 the supervising GP called cardiology, who accepted Adam; the tests were done while the bed was arranged, and question 1 is the formal handover to the admitting registrar. Read the lead, including his repeat observations, hand over all four results together and ask the four questions in order. Adam is present for question 4 and asks his questions if the candidate has not covered them. Credit the X-ray and echo reads (items 23 and 25) in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer; credit aortic valve calcification on the X-ray within item 27 and the absence of hyperinflation within item 28. Credit item 31 if it is given in the ISBAR recommendation. The source expects NYHA class IV, so credit item 26 only for class IV.

The source asked candidates to list investigations and the echo parameters for aortic stenosis. In this format the results are handed over, so those marks become the interpretation items: the systematic echo read (morphology, severity, consequences) in item 25, and the X-ray, ECG and bloods in items 22 to 24. The full investigation list and the detailed comparison of valve options are in the teaching notes and are not marked beyond items 25 and 32.

A high-performing candidate measures the breathlessness by distance, asks directly about orthopnoea, PND, exertional chest pain and syncope, and screens at least five differentials in clusters. They find the slow-rising pulse and the murmur radiating to the carotids. In Part 2 they name severe aortic stenosis from the Doppler numbers and NYHA IV heart failure with preserved EF. They confirm hospital care today and heart team assessment for valve replacement with a tissue valve, advise no driving, and plan care for his son.

A borderline candidate blames his asthma or COPD, misses the triad and the murmur, or reads the echo without stating severity. They may plan an outpatient referral by letter with a routine review.
explain:
Diagnosis: HFpEF secondary to severe calcific aortic stenosis

Adam is 74 and has poorly controlled hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, a 22 pack-year smoking history and a strong family history of coronary disease. His breathlessness has progressed over years and is now brought on by walking 10 m. He has orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, which he does not volunteer. He also has the classic triad of aortic stenosis: exertional breathlessness, exertional chest pain and exertional syncope. His salbutamol does not help, because the problem is not his airways. Examination shows a slow-rising, small-volume pulse and a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with a soft S2, an S4 and a heaving undisplaced apex. There are also signs of congestion: a raised JVP, bibasal crackles and a right pleural effusion. The echo confirms severe aortic stenosis with concentric LVH, preserved ejection fraction and raised filling pressure: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) caused by a pressure-loaded, stiff ventricle.

Quantifying breathlessness and the NYHA class

Ask what the patient can do rather than for a score out of 10: walking up a hill, to the shops or the letterbox, dressing or showering. This shows the impact on daily life and gives the New York Heart Association class:

  • I: no limitation of ordinary activity.
  • II: slight limitation, breathless with ordinary activity.
  • III: marked limitation, breathless with less than ordinary activity.
  • IV: symptoms with any physical activity, or at rest.

Adam is breathless walking 10 m and at rest when lying flat or at night, so the source classes him as NYHA IV.

Aortic stenosis

Aortic stenosis is the most common valve disease in older adults. Causes:

  • Age-related (degenerative) calcific disease: the most common cause in older people, as here.
  • Congenital: a bicuspid valve, or rarely a unicuspid or quadricuspid valve, which presents earlier.
  • Rheumatic: unlikely without mitral disease.

Signs:

  • An ejection systolic (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur loudest in the 2nd intercostal space at the right sternal edge, louder sitting forward in expiration and radiating to the carotids. A musical apical component may occur (the Gallavardin phenomenon).
  • A slow-rising, small-volume carotid pulse.
  • A forceful, sustained apex beat and an S4.
  • A soft or single S2.
  • Basal crackles and effusions when heart failure develops.

A late-peaking murmur, a soft S2 and a slow-rising pulse suggest severe disease; murmur loudness is unreliable. Once symptoms appear, the outlook without valve replacement is poor, which is why symptomatic severe aortic stenosis needs urgent cardiology involvement.

Screening other systems

Group the questions in clusters:

  • Aortic stenosis: exertional syncope and chest pain.
  • Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, dry cough, ankle swelling, right upper quadrant discomfort.
  • ACS or angina; arrhythmia (AF): chest pain, sweating, palpitations.
  • Pleural effusion, pneumonia or TB: fever, sputum, sweats, travel.
  • COPD or asthma: wheeze, chronic cough, smoking.
  • Interstitial lung disease: dry cough, dust exposure.
  • PE: haemoptysis, pleuritic pain, calf swelling.
  • Thyrotoxicosis and anaemia.

Investigations

  • Bloods: FBE (anaemia), BNP (a normal level makes heart failure unlikely), UEC (baseline for diuretics and contrast), LFTs (hepatic congestion), TFTs (thyroid disease).
  • ECG: LVH, ischaemia, AF.
  • Chest X-ray: congestion, effusions, valve calcification, other lung disease. A normal heart size does not exclude HFpEF.
  • Echocardiogram: the main diagnostic test. Transthoracic echo comes first; transoesophageal echo gives more detail of the valve anatomy.

Read the echo in three steps:

  • Valve morphology: thickened, calcified or bicuspid; reduced systolic opening; small orifice.
  • Severity by Doppler: severe aortic stenosis is a peak velocity of 4.0 m/s or more, a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, or a valve area below 1.0 cm² (indexed below 0.6 cm²/m²).
  • Consequences: LV hypertrophy, LV systolic and diastolic function, ejection fraction, left atrial size and pulmonary artery pressure.

Adam meets all three severity criteria.

Differentials

  • Coronary artery disease: he has every risk factor and exertional tightness. Severe aortic stenosis causes angina even with normal coronaries, but coronary angiography is part of the valve work-up.
  • COPD: possible with 22 pack-years, but there is no cough, sputum, wheeze or hyperinflation. Spirometry can be done once he is stable.
  • Asthma: the lack of response to salbutamol, with orthopnoea, argues strongly against it.
  • HFrEF or other valve disease: the EF is preserved and the other valve lesions are mild.
  • PE, pneumonia, anaemia and thyrotoxicosis: the history, examination and bloods do not support them.

Management (NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline; eTG Cardiovascular)

  • Now: NYHA IV heart failure from severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with exertional syncope needs urgent cardiology involvement and hospital care for diuresis and expedited work-up. Discuss him with the cardiology registrar today. While he waits, keep him upright and repeat observations, and give oxygen only to keep SpO2 at 92 to 96% (TSANZ).
  • HFpEF:
    • diuretics for congestion;
    • salt and fluid restriction;
    • daily weights;
    • control of hypertension;
    • treating the cause.
  • Caution in severe aortic stenosis: the hypertrophied ventricle behind a fixed narrow valve depends on its filling pressure. Diurese cautiously, and use vasodilators such as nitrates with caution, as both can cause hypotension and syncope.
  • Definitive treatment: aortic valve replacement, chosen by a heart team (cardiologist and cardiac surgeon). The decision depends on age, surgical risk, frailty, anatomy (including the coronaries and aorta) and the patient's preference. Work-up includes coronary angiography and CT. A dental review before valve replacement reduces the risk of endocarditis.

Valve options

  • TAVI (transcatheter aortic valve implantation): a tissue valve delivered by catheter, usually through the femoral artery. It is less invasive, with a shorter stay and faster recovery. Tissue valves last about 10 to 14 years. Risks include blockage of the coronary ostia and the need for a pacemaker.
  • SAVR (surgical aortic valve replacement): open-heart surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass. There are three kinds of valve:
    • Mechanical: long-lasting, but needs lifelong warfarin.
    • Tissue: lasts about 10 to 14 years without anticoagulation.
    • Ross procedure: the patient's own pulmonary valve is moved to the aortic position and the pulmonary valve is replaced.

Mechanical valves and the Ross procedure are options for younger patients; at Adam's age a tissue valve (TAVI or SAVR) is used.

Every prosthetic valve carries a lifelong risk of endocarditis, and patients with a prosthetic valve need antibiotic prophylaxis for certain dental procedures (eTG).

The person

Adam helps his wife care for their disabled adult son, and the family has limited support. A safe plan for his son has to be made before or during his admission: other family, a hospital social worker, emergency respite, and Carer Gateway. Without it he may refuse to go.

Safety netting

Until the valve is replaced, he should avoid strenuous exertion. Because he has had exertional syncope, he should not drive until he has been assessed and the valve has been treated (Austroads, Assessing Fitness to Drive). He should tell staff immediately while waiting, and call 000 at home, for:

  • fainting or blacking out;
  • chest pain at rest or not settling with rest;
  • breathlessness at rest or getting worse;
  • being unable to lie down;
  • frothy or pink sputum.

After discharge he should weigh himself daily, see his GP within a week, and be referred to a heart failure program, with cardiac rehabilitation after the valve is replaced.
points: Measure breathlessness by what the patient can do (the hill, the letterbox, dressing), not a score out of 10. This gives the NYHA class: walking 10 m with symptoms lying flat and at night is class IV.
Always ask directly about orthopnoea, PND, exertional chest pain and exertional syncope. The triad of exertional breathlessness, angina and syncope means aortic stenosis until proven otherwise.
Aortic stenosis signs are an ejection systolic murmur at the right 2nd intercostal space radiating to the carotids, a slow-rising small-volume pulse, a soft S2, an S4 and a heaving undisplaced apex.

Read the echo by morphology, severity and consequences. Severe aortic stenosis is a peak velocity of 4 m/s or more, a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, or a valve area below 1.0 cm². Concentric LVH with preserved EF and diastolic dysfunction is HFpEF.

Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis needs urgent cardiology involvement and heart team assessment for valve replacement with a tissue valve (TAVI or SAVR) at Adam's age. In the meantime diurese cautiously, because the stiff ventricle depends on its filling pressure, and avoid nitrates.
Plan around the person: a carer admitted to hospital needs a safe plan for the person who depends on them, and exertional syncope means no driving until treated.
